guide.title: Tutorial
guide.stopped: Tutorial stopped. You can reread everything in Settings, Game guide.
guide.paused: The game is paused during the explanation.
guide.indexIntro: Every chapter of the tutorial. Pick one to read it again, even mid-game.

welcome.title: Welcome, founder
welcome.body:
Your startup just raised money. You have 18 months, that is 39 two-week sprints, to make it a success.

This tutorial stays with you for the whole game: each chapter opens when you need it. The game is paused during explanations, so take your time.

HARDCORE.body:
Your startup has just raised money. You have 18 months, that is 39 two-week sprints, to make it a success.

This tutorial stays with you for the whole game: each chapter opens when you need it. Careful: in Hardcore, time never stops during sprints, not even during the explanations.

SHIP_IN_3.body:
Your startup has just raised money. You only have 3 two-week sprints to ship your app.

This tutorial stays with you for the whole game: each chapter opens when you need it. The game is paused during the explanations: take your time.

goal.title: How do you win?
goal.body:
The game ends in one of four ways:

• Bankruptcy: your cash hits zero. Game over.
• IPO: you go public, the best ending. You need to be a Unicorn (a one-billion valuation) with a stable production.
• Acquisition: a big company buys your startup.
• Zombie: after 18 months, you survive without really growing.

Your score is your startup's final valuation.

SHIP_IN_3.body:
In the 3-sprint challenge, the game ends in one of three ways:

• Bankruptcy: your cash reaches zero. Game over.
• Acquisition: at the end of sprint 3, you shipped at least 5 features.
• Zombie: at the end of sprint 3, you shipped fewer than 5.

Your score is your startup's final valuation.

gauges.title: The gauges
gauges.body:
At the top of the screen, the gauges sum up your startup's health. Hover them (or tap them on mobile) to see what they do at any time.

Let's go through them one by one, because the whole game is about keeping them balanced.

treasury.title: Cash
treasury.body:
This is your money. Every month you pay salaries, each dev's costs and the office's fixed costs (€85,000 a month in the garage).

Money comes from your users (about €0.45 per user per month) and from fundraising.

At zero, you go bankrupt and the game ends. Check it before every hire.

coffee.title: Coffee
coffee.body:
Coffee is the team's fuel. Devs drink it while working and during breaks.

Every morning at 8am, the coffee machines refill the stock (it costs money). The more machines you have, the more it refills.

At zero, productivity is divided by 3 and morale drops. A second coffee machine is often a great buy.

debt.title: Tech debt and stability
debt.body:
Tech debt grows when you ship features in a rush. It slows devs down, wears out production and can cause big bugs.

Stability measures how reliable production is. When it drops, outages happen, especially on Friday at 5pm, and users leave.

Refactoring tasks lower the debt; bugfixes and infra raise stability.

hype.title: Hype and users
hype.body:
Hype is how excited investors and the public are about your startup. It goes up when you ship features and slowly goes down every day. At zero, no fundraising is possible.

Users arrive with every shipped feature, and a few on their own when hype is high. They leave when production is unstable. They are the ones who bring in money.

dilemma.title: The big dilemma
dilemma.body:
The whole game fits in one sentence: shipping fast raises the debt, refactoring lowers the hype.

If you only do features, production ends up collapsing. If you only refactor, nobody talks about you anymore. The right rhythm alternates both.

Tip: keep debt under 40 and stability above 60.

easy.title: Easy mode

normal.title: Normal mode

hardcore.title: Hardcore mode
hardcore.body:
No pause. Ever. The pause button and the space bar no longer respond, and even this tutorial cannot stop time: read it while keeping an eye on the office.

The other rules are the Normal ones: €2M, 18 months, at most 3 random cards per sprint.

Tip: time stays stopped during planning and the demo. That is when you think.

hardcoreEvents.title: Crises do not wait
hardcoreEvents.body:
In Hardcore, an event card does not stop time. If you do not choose within 2 in-game hours (about one second at x1), the last answer is picked for you: “you did not decide, so the problem decided for you”.

That last answer is often the worst one. Stay at x1 during office hours so you have time to read, and keep x2 or x4 for nights and weekends.

interns.title: Interns Only mode
interns.body:
Your whole team is made of interns: the starting ones and every hiring candidate.

• They are cheap: about €1,800 per month.
• They are slow and their code creates 40% more debt.
• Each one has a 5% chance per day of breaking prod.

With 6 interns, an outage every three days is normal. Good luck with prod.

internsTips.title: Surviving the interns
internsTips.body:
• Always put bugfix and infra tasks in “To do”: stability is your most fragile gauge.
• Buy a server rack as soon as you can: it raises stability every day.
• Refactor as soon as debt goes above 40.
• Good news: with salaries this low, your cash lasts a long time. Use it to hire.

ship.title: The 3-sprint challenge
ship.body:
“This app must ship in 3 sprints.” The game lasts only 3 sprints instead of 39.

At the end of sprint 3:

• if you shipped at least 5 features, your startup is acquired;
• otherwise, it is the “zombie” ending.

Bankruptcy is still possible, but with €2M it is unlikely in so little time.

shipTips.title: Ship, ship, ship
shipTips.body:
Only features count towards the 5: refactoring, bugfix and infra tasks do not.

• Fill “To do” with small features from the first sprint.
• Hire from the first sprint: every extra dev means more points shipped.
• Do not worry too much about debt: you will not have time to pay for it.

Every demo report shows how many features the sprint shipped.

daily.title: The Daily
daily.body:
The Daily is the same game for everyone, every day, like Wordle. All players start from the same seed: same team, same candidates, same draws. Only your choices make the difference.

The rules are the Normal ones: €2M, 18 months, at most 3 random cards per sprint.

dailyTips.title: Today’s leaderboard
dailyTips.body:
At the end of the game, your score goes to today’s leaderboard if you are signed in. The server replays your whole game from the seed and your decisions to check the score: no cheating possible.

There is no “Play again” button at the end: today’s game is played once. Come back tomorrow for a new seed.

sprint.title: A sprint in 4 parts
sprint.body:
Each sprint lasts two in-game weeks, about 3 real minutes at x1 speed. It has 4 parts:

1. Planning: you choose the work. Time is stopped.
2. Execution: the devs work in the open space.
3. Crises: event cards come up during execution.
4. Demo: the sprint's results.

We are in planning: get your first sprint ready.

openKanban.title: The Kanban
openKanban.body: The Kanban is the board of your product's tasks. This is where you decide what the team works on.
openKanban.do: Open the Kanban with its button (it is blinking).

columns.title: The columns
columns.body:
The board has four columns:

• Backlog: ideas on hold. Nobody touches them.
• To do: the work planned for this sprint.
• Doing: what the devs are working on right now.
• Done: what has shipped.

You only move tasks between Backlog and To do. The devs do the rest on their own.

types.title: Task types
types.body:
Each task has a size in points and a type:

• Feature: brings users and hype, but raises the debt.
• Refactor: melts the debt, but costs a little hype.
• Bugfix: raises stability a lot and lowers the debt a little.
• Infra: raises stability.

The "Impact" line on each card sums up its effect on the gauges.

move.title: Choosing the work
move.body:
Drag a task from Backlog to To do, with your finger or the mouse. You can also use the arrows on the card, or the keyboard.

To start, pick one or two features: you need your first users.

capacity.title: How many tasks?
capacity.body:
Don't overload the sprint. An average dev gets through about 9 points per sprint. A 10x Developer does more than twice that; a Product Owner, half.

What isn't finished at the end of the sprint stays in progress and continues in the next one. Finishing a few tasks beats starting many.

assign.title: Assigning a dev
assign.body:
Devs pick up "To do" tasks on their own. You can still choose who does what: a dev with good Quality creates less debt on a feature.

On the task card, pick a dev in the "Assigned to" list.
assign.do: Assign a task to a dev.

start.title: Here we go
start.body: Everything is ready. The "Start sprint" button starts the execution: the devs get to work and time moves on.
start.do: Close the Kanban and start the sprint.

office.title: Your open space
office.body:
Your devs live in the office: they work, grab coffee, chat, argue, play foosball or fall asleep on the keyboard when they are exhausted. In the evening, they go home.

The bubbles above their heads show what they think. "I'm going to quit" is a warning to take seriously.

speed.title: Game speed
speed.body:
Top right, you set the speed: pause, x1, x2 or x4. The space bar also pauses.

The game is paused during this explanation.
speed.do: Pick a speed, for example x1.

HARDCORE.body:
At the top right, you set the speed: x1, x2 or x4. In Hardcore, pause is disabled.

Time keeps passing during this explanation.
HARDCORE.do: Change the speed, for example to x2.

camera.title: Moving around the office
camera.body:
• Drag to move the camera.
• Mouse wheel or two-finger pinch to zoom.
• Q and E to rotate the view, arrow keys to move with the keyboard.

select.title: Picking a dev
select.body: Click a dev to see their profile (on mobile, long-press them).
select.do: Select a dev in the office.

sheet.title: A dev's profile
sheet.body:
Each dev has four stats:

• Speed: how much work they get through.
• Quality: less debt on their features, more effect from their refactors and bugfixes.
• Endurance: they get tired more slowly.
• Ego: they ask for a higher salary and argue more often.

The profile also shows their morale, energy, personality trait and relationships. They gain experience and levels by working.

roles.title: The 8 profiles
roles.body:
• Bearded Senior: +50% quality, but refuses recent frameworks.
• 10x Developer: very fast, but their code raises the debt.
• Intern: cheap, but a 5% chance per day of breaking production.
• Rustacean: wants to rewrite everything in Rust and converts colleagues.
• Designer: blocks releases if the padding is wrong, but makes demos shine.
• Product Owner: 4 meetings a day (-10% productivity for everyone), but +hype.
• AI Agent: ultra fast, but a 30% chance of hallucinating a feature.
• Ghost Dev: remote, invisible in the office, but their tickets get closed.

INTERNS_ONLY.body:
The game has 8 profiles: Bearded Senior, 10x Developer, Intern, Rustacean, Designer, Product Owner, AI Agent and Ghost Dev.

In this mode you will only meet interns: cheap, motivated, and a 5% chance per day of breaking prod. The 7 other profiles are waiting for you in the other modes.

clock.title: Day, night and Friday 5pm
clock.body:
The clock shows the day and time. The office lighting follows the day/night cycle, and everyone rests at the weekend.

On Friday at 5pm, a banner warns you: it's when production goes down most often if stability is low.

openTeam.title: The team
openTeam.body: The Team panel lists all your devs with their mood, salary and activity.

morale.title: Morale
morale.body:
Each dev has their own morale. It drops with debt, fatigue, lack of coffee and conflicts; it recovers at the weekend, and with plants, foosball or the sofa.

At zero, the dev quits, with a fake LinkedIn post to go with it.

You can fire a dev from their profile: you pay one month of salary and the whole team loses morale, especially their friends.

hiring.title: Making an offer

card.title: An event card
card.body:
During execution, events happen: a broken coffee machine, an investor who wants blockchain, an intern who ran git push --force…

Time stops until you decide. Read the situation, then pick an answer.

HARDCORE.body:
During execution, events happen: a broken coffee machine, an investor who wants blockchain, an intern who ran git push --force…

In Hardcore, time does not stop: you have 2 in-game hours to choose, otherwise the last answer is picked for you. This chapter opens before your first card so you have time to read it.

effects.title: Reading the effects
effects.body:
Under each choice, chips show its effects on the gauges: green for what helps you, red for what costs you.

There is almost never a perfect choice. Ask yourself which gauge you can afford to sacrifice right now.

later.title: "Let's talk about it later"
later.body: Some cards let you postpone the decision. It's tempting, but the card comes back a sprint or two later, worse: its negative effects grow by 50% each time you postpone.

soft.title: In Easy mode
soft.body: In Easy mode, the negative effects of cards are halved (the numbers shown already include it) and at most 2 random cards come up per sprint. Only the Friday 5pm outage can add one.

outage.title: Production incident
outage.body:
The screen flashes red and smoke comes out of the servers: production is down.

An outage costs stability, hype and 2% of your users. The worse your stability and debt, the more often outages happen.

fix.title: Avoiding the next one
fix.body:
Next sprint, put bugfixes and infra in "To do", plus some refactoring if the debt is high.

In the office, a server rack raises stability a little every day, and a trash can nibbles at the debt. And avoid leaving interns alone in charge on Fridays.

report.title: End of the sprint
report.body: The sprint is over: it's demo time. The screen shows the results: users gained or lost, revenue, expenses, features shipped, incidents and valuation.

read.title: Reading the results
read.body:
Compare expenses with revenue: as long as you spend more than you earn, your cash melts. Watch how fast, and raise money before it's too late.

The user feedback at the bottom is mostly there for laughs. Mostly.

next.title: What now?
next.body: The "Next sprint" button opens the planning of the next sprint. Later in the game, this screen can also show an acquisition offer or the IPO button.

openBuild.title: Build mode
openBuild.body: Office items have real effects on the game. You can buy, place, rotate and sell them.

place.title: Placing an item
place.body: Pick an item in the list, then tap a free cell in the office to place it. A €60 plant is a good start.

manage.title: Rotate, move, sell
manage.body:
Click an item already placed to rotate it (R key), move it or sell it. Selling gives back half the purchase price.

Some items only unlock in later phases, when the office grows.

items.title: Useful items
items.body:
• Coffee machine: more coffee every morning. The premium one refills twice as much and lifts morale.
• Plants, rugs, sofa: extra morale.
• Foosball: lots of morale, a bit less productivity.
• Noise-cancelling headsets: cancel the Product Owner's meeting penalty.
• Ergonomic chair and standing desk: devs get tired more slowly.
• Server rack: stability every day.
• Dashboard screen: a little hype every day.

open.title: Tracking progress
open.body: The dashboard plots the history of every gauge, one point per day.

read.title: Reading the charts
read.body: Charts show trends better than a number: debt slowly rising for three sprints means it's time to refactor. Cash on a steep slope means it's time to raise money or slow down hiring.

why.title: Why raise?
why.body: Raising money fills your cash and grows your startup: the 1st round takes you to Seed, the 2nd to Series A. At each phase, the office grows and you can hire more people.

when.title: When to raise?
when.body:
The "Raise funds" button appears during planning, next to "Start sprint".

You need some hype (at zero, no investor will see you), and after each attempt you must wait 3 sprints before the next one. Pick your moment: lots of hype and users is ideal.

pitch.title: The pitch
pitch.body:
In front of the investor, you pick 3 arguments, one per round. Each argument relies on a gauge:

• Traction: you need users.
• Tech: you need low debt.
• Team: you need a large, happy team.
• Stability: some arguments need a reliable production, and the live demo can crash.

Each investor has their own tastes. A failed pitch costs a little hype.

dilution.title: Dilution
dilution.body:
In exchange for the money, the investor takes a share of your startup: between 10 and 30% of the company. The more convinced they are, the more they pay, and the bigger the share they take.

Your share of the company is shown after each round. The more you raise, the smaller it gets.

phases.title: The phases
phases.body:
• Garage: 1 IKEA desk and ramen, 2 people at most.
• Seed (1st round): a small open space, 6 people.
• Series A (2nd round): foosball, plants and standing desks, 15 people.
• Unicorn (one-billion valuation): slide, nap pods and canteen, 30 people.

The valuation depends on your users, your revenue and the team size.

four.title: How it ends
four.body:
After 18 months, your phase decides the ending:

• Unicorn: IPO, the best ending.
• Series A: acquisition, at a discount.
• Seed: acquisition if you are worth more than €100M, otherwise zombie.
• Garage: zombie.

And if your cash hits zero before that, it's bankruptcy.

SHIP_IN_3.body:
The challenge stops at the end of sprint 3:

• at least 5 features shipped: your startup is acquired;
• fewer than 5: it is the “zombie” ending.

And if your cash reaches zero before that, it is bankruptcy. The demo reports show how many features each sprint shipped.

offer.title: Acquisition offers and IPO
offer.body:
From Series A on, a big company may offer to buy you on the demo screen. Accepting ends the game right away with that amount. Refusing means betting on what comes next.

Once you are a Unicorn with a stability of at least 50, the "Launch the IPO" button appears: you can go public without waiting for the end.

share.title: Sharing your ending
share.body: The end screen sums up your game in one sentence ("My startup was acquired for €400M and 7 devs burned out") and offers you an image to share.

slack.title: Slack
slack.body: The Slack panel shows what your devs say in #general, #random and #incidents. It's funny, and it's also a good way to spot who is struggling.

saves.title: Saves
saves.body: The game saves on its own. The Saves panel also lets you save into one of 5 slots and resume later from the menu.

settings.title: Settings
settings.body: In Settings: graphics quality, text size, reduced motion, volumes and the AI-driven Slack. The Game guide is there too: you can reread every chapter of this tutorial whenever you like.

bye.title: You're ready
bye.body:
You now know the whole game. The tutorial ends here: take your startup all the way.

You can reread every chapter at any time in Options, Game guide.

EASY.body:
You now know the whole game. The tutorial ends here: it's up to you to take your startup all the way to the IPO.

When you feel comfortable, try Normal mode, then the Daily to compare yourself with other players.

DAILY.body:
You now know the whole game. The tutorial ends here: go play today’s game.

Compare your score with other players on today’s leaderboard, and come back tomorrow for a new seed.
